subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following represents a straight chain SATURATED hydrocarbon?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
A saturated hydrocarbon is an alkane fitting CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; only C₆H₁₄ satisfies this.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following is a SECONDARY alcohol?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
In CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ the carbon bearing the –OH group is bonded to two other carbon atoms → secondary alcohol.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following is a HYDROLYSIS reaction?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
Hydrolysis of a haloalkane: the halogen (Br) is replaced by –OH using water, forming an alcohol and HBr.

subQuestions.questionText:
Hydrochloric acid reacts with EXCESS zinc:
Zn(s) + 2HCℓ(aq) → ZnCℓ₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Different reaction conditions are shown in the diagrams. The mass of zinc used is the same in both test tubes. Test tube X contains 100 cm³ of 0,1 mol·dm⁻³ HCℓ(aq) with Zn powder. Test tube Y contains 200 cm³ of 0,1 mol·dm⁻³ HCℓ(aq) with Zn lumps. How will the INITIAL rate of reaction and FINAL VOLUME of H₂(g) produced in test tube Y compare with that in test tube X? *(Refer to the two test-tube diagrams in the original question paper.)*

options.A: Initial rate in Y: Higher; Final volume of H₂ in Y: Equal
options.B: Initial rate in Y: Lower; Final volume of H₂ in Y: More
options.C: Initial rate in Y: Lower; Final volume of H₂ in Y: Equal
options.D: Initial rate in Y: Higher; Final volume of H₂ in Y: More

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
Zn lumps have a smaller surface area than powder, so the initial rate in Y is lower. Zn is in excess, so HCℓ is limiting; Y has twice the amount of HCℓ (200 cm³) → more H₂ is produced.

subQuestions.questionText:
The diagram represents a mixture of NO₂(g) and N₂O₄(g) molecules at equilibrium in a 1 dm³ container at T °C. The mixture contains more NO₂ molecules than N₂O₄ molecules. The balanced equation for this reaction is:
2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g)
Which ONE of the following is TRUE for the value of the equilibrium constant, Kc, for the reaction at T °C? *(Refer to the molecule diagram in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
Kc = [N₂O₄]/[NO₂]². Because the container has relatively few N₂O₄ and many NO₂ molecules, the ratio is a small positive value: 0 < Kc < 1.

subQuestions.questionText:
A reaction is at equilibrium in a closed container according to the following balanced equation:
4CuO(s) ⇌ 2Cu₂O(s) + O₂(g)
The volume of the container is now increased while the temperature remains constant. A new equilibrium is reached. Which ONE of the following combinations is CORRECT for the new equilibrium (concentration of O₂ / number of moles of O₂ / equilibrium constant Kc)?

options.A: [O₂] Decreases; moles O₂ Remains the same; Kc Increases
options.B: [O₂] Remains the same; moles O₂ Decreases; Kc Remains the same
options.C: [O₂] Remains the same; moles O₂ Increases; Kc Remains the same
options.D: [O₂] Decreases; moles O₂ Increases; Kc Remains the same

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
Only O₂ is gaseous, so Kc = [O₂]. At constant temperature Kc is unchanged, so [O₂] stays the same; to keep the same concentration in a larger volume the number of moles of O₂ must increase.

subQuestions.questionText:
Nitric acid, HNO₃(aq), and ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH(aq), of equal volumes and concentrations are compared. Consider the following statements regarding these solutions:
(i) They have different pH values.
(ii) Both have the same electrical conductivity.
(iii) Both solutions require the same number of moles of KOH(aq) for complete neutralisation.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are TRUE?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
(i) TRUE – a strong acid and a weak acid of equal concentration have different pH. (iii) TRUE – equal moles of acid require equal moles of KOH. (ii) FALSE – the strong acid ionises more, giving higher conductivity.

subQuestions.questionText: The apparatus in the diagram is used for the titration between HCℓ(aq) and KOH(aq), with HCℓ(aq) in the burette added to the titration mixture. In a titration, the learner accidentally exceeds the endpoint. Which ONE of the following will be TRUE for the titration mixture? *(Refer to the titration apparatus diagram in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
Exceeding the endpoint means excess HCℓ was added, so the mixture becomes acidic: [H⁺] > [OH⁻] and pH < 7.

subQuestions.questionText:
The following hypothetical standard reduction potentials relate to a galvanic cell:
X²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → X(s)   E° = +0,10 V
Y⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Y(s)   E° = −0,10 V
Consider the following statements for this galvanic cell:
(i) The emf of the cell is 0,20 V under standard conditions.
(ii) Electrode Y is the anode.
(iii) X is oxidised.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are TRUE for this galvanic cell?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
(i) TRUE – emf = +0,10 − (−0,10) = 0,20 V. (ii) TRUE – Y has the lower reduction potential, so it is oxidised (anode). (iii) FALSE – X has the higher potential, so it is reduced (cathode), not oxidised.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the half-reactions below will be the MAIN reaction at the ANODE during the electrolysis of CONCENTRATED CuCℓ₂(aq)?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
Oxidation occurs at the anode. In concentrated CuCℓ₂(aq) the high chloride concentration causes chloride to be oxidised: 2Cℓ⁻ → Cℓ₂ + 2e⁻.

subQuestions.questionText:
The relationship between boiling point and molecular mass of aldehydes, carboxylic acids and primary alcohols is investigated. Curves P, R and S are obtained on a graph of boiling point (°C) versus molecular mass (g·mol⁻¹). All compounds used are straight chain molecules. Curve P lies highest, curve R in the middle and curve S lowest. *(Refer to the graph of boiling point versus molecular mass in the original question paper.)*

Define the term boiling point.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
The temperature at which the vapour pressure of a substance equals atmospheric pressure. ✓✓
(If any one of the underlined key phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the conclusion that can be made for curve P.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
OPTION 1 (dependent/independent variables): The higher the molecular mass the higher the boiling point. ✓ OR As the molecular mass increases the boiling point increases. OR The longer the C-chain the higher the boiling point. OR The boiling point and molecular mass are (directly) proportional. ✓ (Dependent and independent variables correctly identified AND correct relationship stated.)
OPTION 2: Curve P represents carboxylic acids. ✓ OR For every molar mass, P has the highest boiling point. ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the answer to QUESTION 3.2 in terms of the structures of the compounds.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
OPTION 1: The strength of the intermolecular forces increases / more sites for London forces with increase of molar mass/chain length/surface area. ✓ More energy is needed to overcome/break the intermolecular forces. ✓
OPTION 2: Curve P / carboxylic acids has the strongest intermolecular forces. ✓ Most energy is needed to overcome/break the intermolecular forces. ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Curve R represents the alcohols. Which homologous series is represented by curve S?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Aldehyde ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the answer to QUESTION 3.4.1 by referring to the strength of intermolecular forces.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
(Comparing the strength of IMF of aldehydes/S with alcohols/R and/or carboxylic acids/P, and linking IMF to boiling point/energy needed.)
Aldehydes/S have the weakest/weaker intermolecular forces. ✓ Therefore aldehydes/S have the lowest/lower boiling points / least/lower energy needed to overcome/break the intermolecular forces. ✓
(Alternatively: carboxylic acids/P and alcohols/R have stronger IMF than aldehydes/S, so they have higher boiling points / need more energy.)

subQuestions.questionText: For curve R, write down the molecular mass of the compound with a boiling point of 97 °C.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
60 (g·mol⁻¹) ✓
Range: 58 – 62 g·mol⁻¹

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the IUPAC name of the compound in QUESTION 3.5.1.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Propan-1-ol / 1-propanol
Mark 1: Correct stem of alcohol, i.e. Propanol. ✓
Mark 2: Correct position of functional group and everything else correct (IUPAC name completely correct including numbering and hyphens). ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Two compounds, A and B, used in this investigation have a molecular mass of 74 g·mol⁻¹. A has a boiling point of 118 °C and B a boiling point of 142 °C. Explain the difference in these boiling points by referring to the structures of these compounds.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Carboxylic acid/B/propanoic acid have (in addition to London forces and dipole-dipole forces) two sites for hydrogen bonding between molecules. ✓ OR carboxylic acid/B can form dimers due to strong hydrogen bonding.
Alcohol/A/butan-1-ol have (in addition to London and dipole-dipole forces) one site for hydrogen bonding between molecules. ✓
Intermolecular forces in the carboxylic acid are stronger / more energy is needed to overcome/break the intermolecular forces in the carboxylic acid, so it has the higher boiling point. ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the cracking reaction below:
C₁₆H₃₄ → C₆H₁₄ + C₆Hₓ + 2CᵧHᵤ

Define cracking.

The chemical process/reaction in which longer chain hydrocarbon/alkane molecules are broken down to shorter (more useful) molecules. ✓✓
(If any one of the underlined key phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the values represented by x, y and z in the equation C₁₆H₃₄ → C₆H₁₄ + C₆Hₓ + 2CᵧHᵤ (where the third product is 2CᵧHᵤ).

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the equations for reactions I to III below. A and B represent organic compounds that are POSITIONAL ISOMERS. X is an inorganic product.
I: CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₃ + HCℓ → A + B
II: A + H₂O → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ + X
III: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₃ + H₂O

Write down the definition of positional isomers.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Compounds with the same molecular formula, but different positions of the side chain / substituents / functional groups on the parent chain. ✓✓
(If any one of the underlined key phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the type of reaction represented by reaction I.

Addition / hydrohalogenation / hydrochlorination ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the STRUCTURAL formula of compound B.

Mark 3: Whole structure correct. ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the formula of X.

HCℓ ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the inorganic reagent for reaction III.
subQuestions.memoText:

(Concentrated) H₂SO₄ / sulphuric acid / H₃PO₄ / phosphoric acid ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Compound A can be converted directly to the organic product of reaction III. Besides heat, write down the reaction condition needed for this conversion.

Elimination ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
The reaction between EXCESS dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium thiosulphate is used to investigate factors that influence reaction rate:
Na₂S₂O₃(aq) + 2HCℓ(aq) → 2NaCℓ(aq) + S(s) + H₂O(ℓ) + SO₂(g)
The concentration of HCℓ(aq) used is 1 mol·dm⁻³. The same volume of HCℓ(aq) is used in each run. The time taken for the cross on the paper under the flask to become invisible is measured. The results are:
Run 1: 50 cm³ Na₂S₂O₃(aq), 0 cm³ H₂O added, concentration 0,13 mol·dm⁻³, time 20,4 s.
Run 2: 40 cm³ Na₂S₂O₃(aq), 10 cm³ H₂O added, concentration 0,10 mol·dm⁻³, time 26,7 s.
Run 3: 30 cm³ Na₂S₂O₃(aq), 20 cm³ H₂O added, concentration P, time 33,3 s.
*(Refer to the apparatus diagram and results table in the original question paper.)*

Define reaction rate.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks, 2 or 0):
ANY ONE:
• Change in concentration of products/reactants per (unit) time.
• Change in amount/number of moles/volume/mass of products or reactants per (unit) time.
• Amount/number of moles/volume/mass of products formed/reactants used per (unit) time.
• Rate of change in concentration/amount/number of moles/volume/mass. ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the independent variable for this investigation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Concentration (of Na₂S₂O₃) ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the value of P in the table.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Using dilution c₁V₁ = c₂V₂:
(0,13)(0,030) = c₂(0,050) ✓ (substitute 0,03 and 0,13; substitute 0,05)
c₂ = 0,078 mol·dm⁻³ ✓✓
Range: 0,075 to 0,08 mol·dm⁻³.

subQuestions.questionText: When 0,21 g of sulphur has formed in Run 1, the cross becomes invisible. Calculate the average reaction rate with respect to sodium thiosulphate, Na₂S₂O₃(aq), in g·s⁻¹.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
n(S) = m/M = 0,21/32 ✓ (substitute M = 32 g·mol⁻¹) = 0,00656 mol
Use mole ratio n(S) = n(Na₂S₂O₃) = 0,00656 mol ✓
m(Na₂S₂O₃) = n × M = 0,00656 × 158 ✓ (substitute M = 158 g·mol⁻¹) = 1,04 g
Rate = m/t = 1,04/20,4 ✓ (divide by 20,4 s)
Rate = 0,051 g·s⁻¹ ✓
Range: 0,048 to 0,080 g·s⁻¹.

subQuestions.questionText: Another investigation is performed at different temperatures. Sketch the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve for the reaction at 20 °C. Label this curve as A. On the same set of axes, draw the curve that will be obtained at 35 °C and label it as B. *(A Maxwell-Boltzmann sketch is required as the answer; refer to the marking guideline in the original memo.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Both axes labelled correctly (number of particles/molecules vs kinetic energy). ✓
Mark 2: Both curves start at the origin and have the correct shape. ✓
Mark 3: Peak of curve B (35 °C) must be lower than curve A (20 °C). ✓
Mark 4: Curve B must have higher kinetic energy than curve A from the peak up to the end of curve B (B shifted to the right). ✓
IF curves not labelled: Max. 3/4.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the effect of temperature on reaction rate in terms of the collision theory.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
At a higher temperature particles move faster / have higher kinetic energy. ✓
More molecules have enough/sufficient kinetic energy for an effective collision (OR more molecules have kinetic energy ≥ the activation energy). ✓
More effective collisions per unit time/second (OR frequency of effective collisions increases). ✓
Reaction rate increases. ✓
(A converse argument for lower temperature is equally acceptable.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the following hypothetical reaction reaching equilibrium in a 4 dm³ closed container at 150 °C:
2AB(g) ⇌ A₂(g) + B₂(g)
A graph shows the changes in the amounts (number of moles) of reactants and products over time (0 to 160 s). AB(g) is the upper curve, A₂(g) an intermediate curve and B₂(g) a lower curve; a change is made at t = 80 s and a new equilibrium is reached. *(Refer to the graph of number of moles versus time in the original question paper.)*

Write down the meaning of the term reversible reaction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
A reaction where products can be converted back to reactants (and vice versa). ✓ OR both forward and reverse reactions can take place / a reaction which can take place in both directions.

subQuestions.questionText: State Le Chatelier's principle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
When the equilibrium in a closed system is disturbed, the system will re-instate a new equilibrium by favouring the reaction that will cancel/oppose the disturbance. ✓✓
(If any one of the underlined key phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.)

subQuestions.questionText: A change was made to the equilibrium mixture at t = 80 s. Write down the change made at t = 80 s.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
The amount/concentration of A₂(g) was increased / A₂ was added to the container. ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain how the system reacts to this change.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
The increase in A₂/concentration favours the reaction that uses or decreases the amount/concentration of A₂. ✓ The reverse reaction is favoured. ✓ (OR amount/concentration of products decreases OR amount/concentration of reactants increases.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the equilibrium constant, Kc, at t = 120 s. (The equilibrium amounts of AB, A₂ and B₂ are read from the graph and the container volume is 4 dm³.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Kc expression: Kc = [A₂][B₂]/[AB]² ✓
Convert the equilibrium moles read from the graph to concentrations (÷ 4 dm³) and substitute. ✓✓
Kc = 0,16 ✓ (OPTION 1/2). An alternative reading of the graph gives Kc = 0,44 (OPTION 3/4).
IF wrong Kc expression: Max. 2/4. IF no Kc expression: Max. 3/4.
*(Exact equilibrium values are read from the graph in the original question paper.)*

subQuestions.questionText: At t = 130 s the temperature of the system is decreased to 100 °C. Draw a potential energy diagram for this reaction. *(A potential energy diagram is required as the answer; refer to the marking guideline in the original memo.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Both axes correctly labelled (potential energy vs course of reaction; accept time). ✓
Mark 2 & 3: Correct shape of the Ep curve for an endothermic reaction (products at higher potential energy than reactants, with an activation-energy hump). ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Will the equilibrium constant, Kc, at 100 °C be GREATER THAN, LESS THAN or EQUAL TO the Kc at 150 °C? Explain the answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Less than ✓
The amount/concentration of products/B₂/A₂ decreases ✓ (OR amount/concentration of reactants/AB increases OR the reverse reaction is favoured / equilibrium position shifts to the left). ✓
(A decrease in temperature favours the exothermic reverse reaction of this endothermic forward reaction, so Kc decreases.)

subQuestions.questionText: The initial reaction now takes place in the presence of a catalyst at 150 °C. Describe the changes that will be observed on the graph between t = 0 s and t = 60 s.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
The gradients (of all three curves) will be steeper ✓ and reach the same equilibrium values ✓ before 40 s / reaches the same equilibrium sooner (in less than 40 s). ✓
OR the gradients of the curves become zero at the same equilibrium values before 40 s.
IF curves are identified, all three must be named.

subQuestions.questionText:
To identify metal M in an unknown metal carbonate, MCO₃, the following procedure is carried out:
Step 1: 0,198 g of IMPURE MCO₃ is reacted with 25 cm³ of 0,4 mol·dm⁻³ nitric acid, HNO₃(aq).
Step 2: The EXCESS HNO₃(aq) is then neutralised with 20 cm³ of 0,15 mol·dm⁻³ barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂(aq).
Assume that the volumes are additive. The following reactions take place:
2HNO₃(aq) + MCO₃(s) → M(NO₃)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(ℓ)
2HNO₃(aq) + Ba(OH)₂(aq) → Ba(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2H₂O(ℓ)

Define the term strong base.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
A strong base (ionises) dissociates completely in water to form a high concentration of OH⁻ ions. ✓✓
ACCEPT: A strong base (ionises) dissociates completely in water.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the number of moles of Ba(OH)₂(aq) that reacted with the excess HNO₃(aq).
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
n(Ba(OH)₂) = cV ✓
= (0,15)(0,02) ✓
= 0,003 mol ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the pH of the solution after Step 1.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
(Positive marking from 7.2.1.)
n(HNO₃) excess = 2 × n(Ba(OH)₂) = 2(0,003) = 0,006 mol ✓ (use ratio 2n(Ba(OH)₂) = n(HNO₃))
n(H₃O⁺) = n(HNO₃) = 0,006 mol
[H₃O⁺] = n/V = 0,006/0,025 ✓ (substitute 0,025 dm³) = 0,24 mol·dm⁻³
pH = −log[H₃O⁺] ✓ = −log(0,24) ✓
pH = 0,62 ✓

subQuestions.questionText: The percentage purity of the MCO₃(s) in the sample is 85%. Identify metal M.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (8 marks):
(Positive marking from 7.2.2.)
n(HNO₃)initial = cV = (0,4)(0,025) ✓ = 0,01 mol
n(HNO₃) reacted with MCO₃ = n(HNO₃)initial − n(HNO₃)excess = 0,01 − 0,006 ✓ = 0,004 mol
n(MCO₃) = ½ n(HNO₃) = ½(0,004) ✓ = 0,002 mol (use ratio)
m(MCO₃ pure) = 0,85 × 0,198 ✓ = 0,168 g (calculate pure mass)
M(MCO₃) = m/n = 0,168/0,002 ✓ (substitute n and m) = 84 g·mol⁻¹
Molar mass of M = 84 − 60 ✓ (subtract 60 g·mol⁻¹ for CO₃) = 24 g·mol⁻¹
Therefore metal M is Mg. ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
A cleaned pure copper strip, Cu(s), is placed in a beaker containing a colourless silver nitrate solution, AgNO₃(aq), at 25 °C. After a while, it is observed that the solution in the beaker becomes blue. *(Refer to the beaker diagram in the original question paper.)*

Write down ONE other OBSERVABLE change, besides the solution turning blue.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Copper strip becomes thinner / corrodes / decreases in mass / solid (silver-coloured) particles in solution / the copper becomes plated with silver. ✓
IF rust: 0/1.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the NAME or FORMULA of the oxidising agent.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Ag⁺ (ion) / silver ion / AgNO₃ / silver nitrate ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the answer to QUESTION 8.1.1 by referring to the relative strengths of the oxidising agents or reducing agents.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Ag⁺ (ion) is a stronger oxidising agent than Cu²⁺ ion ✓ and will oxidise Cu ✓ to Cu²⁺ ion. ✓
OR Cu²⁺ (ion) is a weaker oxidising agent than Ag⁺ ion and Cu will be oxidised to Cu²⁺ ion.
OR Cu/copper is a stronger reducing agent than Ag/silver and will reduce silver ions to silver.

subQuestions.questionText:
A galvanic cell is now set up using Cu and Ag strips as electrodes. A simplified diagram of the cell is shown with a voltmeter (V), electrode A in silver ion solution Ag⁺(aq), and electrode B in solution B. *(Refer to the galvanic cell diagram in the original question paper.)*

Write down the NAME or FORMULA of electrode A.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Silver / Ag ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the NAME or FORMULA of solution B.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
CuSO₄ / Cu²⁺ / copper(II) ions / copper(II) sulphate ✓
ACCEPT: any soluble copper(II) salt e.g. Cu(NO₃)₂.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the overall (net) balanced equation for the cell reaction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
2Ag⁺(aq) + Cu(s) → 2Ag(s) + Cu²⁺(aq)
Mark 1: Reactants. ✓
Mark 2: Products. ✓
Mark 3: Balancing. ✓
Ignore double arrows and phases.

subQuestions.questionText: The salt bridge contains potassium nitrate, KNO₃(aq). Write down the FORMULA of the ion in the salt bridge that will move into the silver ion solution. Choose from K⁺(aq) or NO₃⁻(aq). Give a reason for the answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
K⁺ ✓
[Ag⁺] decreases (in the silver half-cell the concentration of positive ions decreases / the silver half-cell becomes negative), so K⁺ moves in to maintain the ion balance / electrical neutrality. ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
An electrolytic cell is set up to purify a piece of copper that contains silver and zinc as impurities. A simplified diagram of the cell is shown, connected to a power source; electrode R is the impure copper and electrode Q is in the electrolyte. *(Refer to the electrolytic cell diagram in the original question paper.)*

Define the term electrolysis.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks, 2 or 0):
ANY ONE:
• The chemical process in which electrical energy is converted to chemical energy.
• The use of electrical energy to produce a chemical change.
• Decomposition of an ionic compound by means of electrical energy.
• The process during which an electric current passes through a solution/ionic liquid/molten ionic compound. ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the reaction taking place at electrode Q.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) ✓✓
ACCEPT: Reduction (reaction). Ignore phases. If the charge (+) is omitted on Cu²⁺: Max. 1/2.

subQuestions.questionText: In which direction do the electrons flow in the external circuit? Choose from Q to R or R to Q.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
R to Q ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the current needed to form 16 g of copper when the cell operates for five hours.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
n(Cu) = m/M = 16/63,5 ✓ (substitute 63,5) = 0,25 mol
N(Cu atoms) = n × Nₐ = 0,25 × 6,02 × 10²³ ✓ (substitute 6,02 × 10²³) = 1,5 × 10²³
n(electrons) = N(Cu atoms) × 2 = (1,5 × 10²³)(2) ✓ = 3 × 10²³ electrons
Q = n(e) × charge = (3 × 10²³)(1,6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 48 160 C
t = (5)(60)(60) = 18 000 s ✓
I = Q/t = 48 160/18 000 = 2,68 A ✓
Range: 1,34 to 2,70 A (1,34 A if Cu⁺ is assumed).

subQuestions.questionText: During this electrolysis, only copper and zinc are oxidised. Give a reason why the silver is not oxidised.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Ag/silver is a weaker reducing agent than Cu/copper or Zn/zinc ✓ and will not be oxidised. ✓
OR Cu/copper or Zn/zinc is a stronger reducing agent than Ag/silver and Ag will not be oxidised.
OR the voltage of the power source is not effective enough to oxidise Ag/silver.
